client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup a few months ago. It feels like no matter how hard I try, I'm always behind on something — there's always another deadline looming and I never feel like I'm actually catching up. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a real sense of exhaustion and defeat — like you're running hard on a treadmill that just keeps speeding up, and even this conversation feels like it might not be worth the effort. That feeling of skepticism makes a lot of sense when you're in the thick of it, and I want you to know we can work with that doubt rather than push it aside. I'm curious — when you imagine "catching up," what does that actually look like for you, and do you think that picture might be shaping how you measure yourself each day?

client: Honestly, when I picture "catching up," it's like... getting to a point where my inbox is empty, my apartment is clean, my deadlines are all met, and I can finally just breathe without that tight feeling in my chest. But even saying that out loud, I realize it sounds kind of impossible, like that moment never actually arrives. I guess I measure every day by how far I am from that imaginary finish line, and most days I feel like I'm losing ground.
therapist: There's something really important in what you just noticed yourself — that the finish line you're measuring yourself against might be more of a mirage than a real destination, and that awareness took courage to say out loud. When every day is graded against a perfect, everything-resolved moment, it's almost guaranteed to feel like falling short, even on days when you actually did a lot. What do you think it would feel like to measure a day by what you *did* move forward, even just a little, rather than how far you still are from that imaginary finish line?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it could feel better that way. But honestly, when I try to think about measuring a day by small progress, it just feels like I'm lowering the bar for myself, like I'm giving myself permission to be mediocre. I guess I'm scared that if I stop holding myself to that high standard, I'll just... stop trying altogether.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — there's a part of you that's been using that high standard as a kind of engine, and it's scary to imagine what happens if you loosen your grip on it. But I'd gently invite you to look at the evidence: that relentless standard has been running for a while now, and instead of driving you forward, it seems to be leaving you exhausted and feeling like you're always losing. What if the standard isn't actually what's keeping you motivated — what else in your life, or in this work, might genuinely drive you if the fear wasn't doing all the heavy lifting?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with it, but honestly I'm not sure there's much else there. Like, when I try to think about what would motivate me without the fear of failing or letting people down, I just kind of... draw a blank, and that actually scares me more. What if the fear really is the only thing keeping me going, and without it I just stop trying altogether?
therapist: It makes sense that drawing that blank feels unsettling — it's like peering into a room you've never really been allowed to enter, because fear has been guarding the door for so long. But I'd gently push back on the idea that the blank means nothing is there; it might just mean that the things that genuinely matter to you have been drowned out by the noise of pressure and anxiety for a while. Can you think of a time, even early in your career or in your life, when you worked hard at something not because you were afraid, but because something about it just pulled you in?

client: I actually had to sit with that question for a second, because my first instinct was to say "I don't know" again. But there was this one project early on, maybe seven or eight years into my career, where I stayed late not because I was worried about my boss noticing but because I genuinely wanted to see how it turned out. I haven't thought about that in a long time, and it's a little strange to realize how far away that feeling seems now.
therapist: That memory is really significant — you just proved to yourself that the blank isn't actually empty, that there's a version of you who was genuinely pulled toward something rather than pushed by fear. It makes sense that reconnecting with that feeling brings a kind of quiet wistfulness, like spotting something you didn't realize you'd lost. What do you think was different about that project — what was it about the work itself that made you want to stay and see it through?

client: I think it was because nobody was watching, really — there were no deadlines, no one grading me, so I wasn't performing for anyone. I just got absorbed in figuring out how the pieces fit together, and time kind of disappeared. But honestly, even saying that out loud makes me feel a little sad, because it feels so far away from how I approach anything now.
therapist: There's a gentle sadness in what you're sharing, like you're looking at an old photograph of yourself and feeling the distance from that person — and that grief is worth honoring, because it means something real mattered to you then and probably still does. What you're describing — that absorption, time disappearing, figuring out how pieces fit — that's not a personality you lost, it's more likely one that got buried under years of pressure and performance. I'm wondering, in your current work, even in small moments, are there any flickers of that same puzzle-solving pull, however faint they might feel right now?

client: I sat with that for a second, because honestly it's the first thing anyone's said in a while that didn't feel like a pep talk. Maybe there are small moments, like when a system breaks down at work and I'm the one tracing it back to the source, there's something that kicks in that feels almost automatic. But then the moment passes and it's back to just... grinding through the day, and I wonder if one flicker here and there is really enough to hold onto.
therapist: That flicker you just described — something kicking in automatically when a system breaks down — that's not nothing, that's actually a glimpse of your natural wiring showing through the grind, and it's the same person who stayed late all those years ago. You're right that one flicker doesn't transform everything overnight, but in CBT we often find that these small moments are data points worth paying attention to, because they point toward what genuinely engages you beneath all the noise. I'm curious — what would it look like to deliberately put yourself in the path of more of those moments, even in small ways, rather than waiting for them to happen by chance?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that flicker means something real. But honestly, the idea of deliberately putting myself in those situations feels kind of forced, like I'd be manufacturing something that's supposed to happen naturally. And what if I set it up and the spark just... doesn't show up? That feels like it would make things worse, not better.
therapist: There's a quiet but real fear underneath what you're saying — not panic, but a kind of careful self-protection, like you'd rather not reach for something than risk confirming it's gone. That makes a lot of sense, and it's worth naming that the thought "if I try and it doesn't work, that proves something is broken" is actually a belief worth examining, not a fact. What's the evidence that the spark not showing up in one deliberate moment would mean it's gone for good, versus just having an off day?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like, one bad attempt doesn't equal permanent damage. But it's hard to separate that in the moment, because it's not just one moment, it's been weeks of feeling this way, and that pattern is what scares me. What if it's not an off day but an off season, or worse?
therapist: What you're describing — weeks of this weighing on you, the fear that it's not temporary but something deeper — that's a genuinely heavy thing to carry, and it makes sense that the logical reframe doesn't just dissolve that worry. But I want to gently reflect something back: you came here today skeptical that talking would help, and yet in this conversation you remembered a version of yourself you hadn't thought about in years, and found a flicker you hadn't named before — that's not nothing, even in the middle of an "off season." I'm wondering, when you imagine this being a season rather than permanent, what would it look like for this season to eventually shift — what would you notice first?

client: I guess... the first thing I'd notice is probably just waking up and not immediately feeling that dread, that heavy kind of "here we go again" feeling before the day even starts. Like, right now mornings are the worst part, and I imagine in a better season I'd just wake up and feel kind of neutral, maybe even curious about the day instead of already exhausted by it. But even as I say that, part of me wonders if I'm just describing something I used to have and lost, not something I can actually get back.
therapist: The way you described that — waking up curious instead of braced for impact — was so specific and alive that it didn't sound like an abstract wish, it sounded like a memory your body still knows how to feel. And that distinction you're wrestling with, "something I lost versus something I can get back," is actually one of the most important questions we could sit with together, because lost and buried are very different things. Given everything you've uncovered today about that version of yourself, what would it take for you to hold even a small amount of openness to the possibility that it's buried rather than gone?
